mathprize-olympiad-2014-01.title: Perpendicular diagonals, then lengths
mathprize-olympiad-2014-01.body:
Let $ABCD$ be tasty and let the diagonals meet at $P$.

**Diagonals are perpendicular.** $\angle APB$ is an exterior angle of triangle $BPC$, so it is larger than $\angle PBC$ and $\angle PCB$. Triangles $APB$ and $BPC$ are similar, so $\angle APB$ equals one of the three angles of triangle $BPC$; it exceeds two of them, hence $\angle APB=\angle BPC$. These angles are supplementary, so both are $90^\circ$. Thus $AC\perp BD$.

**Lengths.** By symmetry of the labelling assume $AP$ is the smallest of $AP,BP,CP,DP$ and scale so that $AP=1$. Put $BP=r\ge1$. Right triangles $APB$ (legs $1,r$) and $DPA$ (legs $1,DP$) are similar, so $DP\in\{r,1/r\}$; since $DP\ge1$, $DP=r$. Then $\triangle APB\cong\triangle APD$ (SAS), so $AB=AD$; and $\triangle CPB\cong\triangle CPD$ (SAS, $BP=DP$, common leg $CP$), so $CB=CD$. Hence $ABCD$ is a kite with axis $AC$.

Right triangle $BPC$ (legs $r,CP$) is similar to $APB$ (legs $1,r$). Matching the legs, either $CP=1$ or $CP=r^2$.

- If $CP=1$: $AP=CP$ and $BP=DP$ with perpendicular diagonals, so $ABCD$ is a rhombus.
- If $CP=r^2$: the similarity $\triangle APB\sim\triangle BPC$ (with $A\to B$, $P\to P$, $B\to C$) gives $\angle PAB=\angle PBC$. Since $\angle PAB+\angle PBA=90^\circ$, we get $\angle PBA+\angle PBC=90^\circ$, i.e. $\angle ABC=90^\circ$. By the symmetry of the kite $\angle ADC=90^\circ$ too. So $ABCD$ is a kite with two opposite right angles (a *right kite*).

**Converse.** In a rhombus the diagonals bisect each other and the sides are equal, so by SSS the four triangles are congruent, hence similar. In a right kite $ABCD$ ($\angle B=\angle D=90^\circ$, $AB=AD$, $CB=CD$) the diagonal $AC$ cuts it into two congruent right triangles, and the diagonal $BD$ (perpendicular to $AC$) is the altitude to the hypotenuse in each; the altitude to the hypotenuse splits a right triangle into two triangles similar to it. So all four pieces are similar.

**Answer:** the tasty convex quadrilaterals are exactly the rhombuses and the right kites. ∎

mathprize-olympiad-2014-02.title: Trigonometric substitution
mathprize-olympiad-2014-02.body:
Since $f(\sin^2\theta)=4\sin^2\theta\cos^2\theta=\sin^22\theta$, define
$$x_i=\sin^2\!\left(2^{i-1}\alpha\right),\qquad\alpha=\frac{\pi}{2^n+1}.$$
Then $f(x_i)=\sin^2(2^i\alpha)=x_{i+1}$ for $1\le i\le n-1$. Also
$$f(x_n)=\sin^2(2^n\alpha)=\sin^2(\pi-\alpha)=\sin^2\alpha=x_1,$$
since $2^n\alpha=\pi-\alpha$.

**Distinctness.** We have $0<\alpha<2\alpha<\dots<2^{n-1}\alpha=\frac{2^{n-1}\pi}{2^n+1}<\frac\pi2$. Since $\sin^2$ is strictly increasing on $[0,\frac\pi2]$, $x_1<x_2<\dots<x_n$, so they are distinct. ∎

mathprize-olympiad-2014-03.title: Sparse sum in base 100
mathprize-olympiad-2014-03.body:
Let $a_i=4^i$ for $i=1,\dots,1007$ and
$$n=2\sum_{i=1}^{1007}100^{a_i}.$$
Its digits are $1007$ twos and zeros, so $n$ is sweet with digit sum $2014$.

**Distinct sums.** For indices $i\le j$ the sums $a_i+a_j$ are pairwise distinct, and for $i\le j\le k$ the sums $a_i+a_j+a_k$ are pairwise distinct: a sum of at most three powers of $4$ has at most three equal powers, so every base-$4$ digit is at most $3$ and the representation is unique; it determines the multiset of powers. The same holds for $2a_i+a_j$ ($i\ne j$) as the multiset $\{i,i,j\}$.

**Square.**
$$n^2=4\sum_i100^{2a_i}+8\sum_{i<j}100^{a_i+a_j}.$$
All exponents here are distinct, and the coefficients $4$ and $8$ are less than $100$, so in base $100$ (each base-100 place is two decimal digits) the digits of $n^2$ are $04$, $08$ and $00$: only the digits $0,4,8$ appear. So $n^2$ is sweet.

**Cube.**
$$n^3=8\sum_i100^{3a_i}+24\sum_{i\ne j}100^{2a_i+a_j}+48\sum_{i<j<k}100^{a_i+a_j+a_k}.$$
The exponents $3a_i$, $2a_i+a_j$ ($i\ne j$, ordered), $a_i+a_j+a_k$ ($i<j<k$) correspond to different multisets of three indices, hence are all distinct. The coefficients $8,24,48$ are less than $100$, so the decimal digits of $n^3$ are among $0,8,2,4$ ($08$, $24$, $48$, $00$). So $n^3$ is sweet. ∎

mathprize-olympiad-2014-04.title: Redistribute black squares by columns
mathprize-olympiad-2014-04.body:
Look at the $n$ columns (each with $4$ squares). We show that the black squares can be moved so that every column has at least one; the total number is unchanged, so it is at least $n$.

**An all-white column has rich neighbours.** In an all-white column, each of the $4$ squares can only be next to a black square in the left or right neighbouring column (same row). So the left and right neighbours together contain at least $4$ black squares (at a boundary, the only neighbour has $4$). Therefore either the left neighbour has at least $3$ black squares, or the right neighbour has at least $2$ (if the left one has at most $2$, the right one has at least $2$).

In particular, the neighbours of an all-white column are not all-white.

**Moving.** Each all-white column takes one black square (counted, not literal position) from its left neighbour if that neighbour has at least $3$ black squares, and otherwise from its right neighbour, which then has at least $2$.

**Every column ends nonempty.**
- An originally all-white column received one.
- A column with $1$ black square gives none away: donors have at least $3$ (left donor) or at least $2$ (right donor).
- A column with $2$ black squares can only be a right-neighbour donor for the column on its left, and it is a donor for its right neighbour only if it has $\ge3$; so it gives at most $1$ and keeps at least $1$.
- A column with $3$ or $4$ black squares gives at most one to each side, so keeps at least $1$.

(All-white columns are never donors, as their neighbours are not all-white and a donor needs black squares.) So after moving, every column has at least one black square, and the total number of black squares is unchanged. Hence there are at least $n$. ∎
